analysis.one_liner: Guarantees employees up to twelve weeks of unpaid leave for births, adoptions, and serious family illness.
analysis.headline: Referred to three House committees and four subcommittees after introduction in February 1992, the bill never received a hearing, committee vote, or floor vote before the 102nd Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required employers with 50 or more workers (100 during the first two years) to give qualifying employees up to 12 weeks of unpaid leave for the birth or adoption of a child, 6 weeks to care for a seriously ill spouse, child, or parent, and 6 weeks for the employee's own serious health condition. Workers on leave would keep their health insurance and get their job or an equivalent one back. It would have covered federal civil service workers and even House and Senate employees themselves.
analysis.who_benefits: Employees of larger employers who have worked at least 12 months and 1,250 hours: new and adoptive parents, workers facing serious illness, and people caring for a sick spouse, child, or parent. The bill would let them take leave without losing their job or health coverage.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Parents and workers facing serious illness

how_it_helps.text: Entitles eligible employees to 12 workweeks of leave for the birth or adoption of a child, and 6 workweeks for their own or a family member's serious health condition, within any 12-month period [S2][S3].
Requires the employer to restore the employee to their original job or an equivalent one with equivalent pay and benefits, and to maintain group health coverage during unpaid leave [S2][S3].

Prohibits employers from interfering with leave rights or retaliating against workers who assert them, with damages including liquidated double recovery and attorney's fees, enforced through Labor Department investigation and private lawsuits [S2][S3].
Extends the same leave rights to federal civil service employees and to employees of the House and Senate, applying Title I protections to congressional offices [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Employers with 50 or more employees (100 during the first two years) bear the cost: holding jobs open, maintaining health insurance premiums during unpaid leave, certification and compliance paperwork, and exposure to lawsuits with double damages and fee-shifting if they violate the law.

drawbacks.text: The leave is unpaid unless the employee substitutes accrued paid vacation or sick leave, so many workers who cannot afford weeks without a paycheck would get little practical benefit [S2][S3].
Employers with fewer than 50 employees within 50 miles of a worksite are excluded, so employees of small businesses get no federal leave right at all [S2][S3].

Employers gain broad defenses: they can demand medical certification and second and third opinions, require temporary transfers for intermittent leave, deny reinstatement to the highest-paid 10 percent of workers, and recover health premiums from employees who do not return [S2][S3].

Employers take on litigation risk, with damages that include an equal amount of liquidated damages plus attorney's fees, and spouses at the same employer can have their combined leave capped at 12 weeks [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offers a real but modest guarantee: job security around births, adoptions, and illness, with health coverage intact. Because the leave is unpaid and smaller employers are exempt, its practical reach is limited, and honest supporters would acknowledge the compliance and litigation burden it places on employers. The structure, including the employer safeguards, closely tracks what Congress ultimately enacted as the Family and Medical Leave Act in 1993.

outcome.mechanism: After introduction the bill was split among three committees and sent to four subcommittees, and none of them acted before the 102nd Congress expired in January 1993, so the bill simply died.

narrative.text: Representative Tim Penny introduced the bill on February 25, 1992, with no cosponsors [S1][S4].
The same day it was referred jointly to the Committees on Education and Labor, House Administration, and Post Office and Civil Service [S5].
In March 1992 it was referred to four subcommittees: Compensation and Employee Benefits, Personnel and Police, Labor Standards, and Labor-Management Relations [S5].
No further action appears in the record; no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote ever took place, and the bill died when the 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large employers avoided the leave mandate for a few months, but the delay was short: a near-identical family and medical leave bill was enacted by the next Congress and signed into law in February 1993, so workers ultimately received the same protections through a different vehicle. This particular bill's death mattered mainly because it was one of many stalled vehicles in a fight that dragged through the 101st and 102nd Congresses while an earlier version that passed Congress was rejected by President George H.W. Bush.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers briefly, until the same law passed in 1993

sides.party_line_note: There were no roll-call votes and the bill drew no cosponsors, so no party split appears in the record; the bill's fate was decided by committee inaction, and the broader family leave fight of that era split mostly along party lines, with Democrats supporting mandated leave and President Bush vetoing an earlier version.

industries.note: Covered employers would have to hold jobs open for up to 12 weeks of unpaid leave, keep paying health insurance premiums during leave, and face double damages and attorney's fees if they denied leave or retaliated. Their cost is the benefit workers receive, so their interest in this bill ran against ordinary employees.

industries.industry: Small employers (fewer than 50 workers within 50 miles)
industries.note: The bill exempted worksites with fewer than 50 employees within 50 miles (100 during the first two years), so their workers would receive no federal leave right even as larger firms complied.

industries.industry: Employer group health plans and insurers
industries.note: Plans would have to keep covering employees on unpaid leave, but employers could recover the premiums paid if the employee never returned to work, so the added cost is temporary and limited.
